description.en: The winner and the host country (or countries) of every FIFA World Cup, the men's tournament from 1930 to 2026 (23 tournaments) and the women's from 1991 to 2023 (9 tournaments): 64 cards. Front: the tournament and the question, e.g. "FIFA World Cup 1958: winner" or "FIFA Women's World Cup 2023: host"; back: the country in English and Swedish. Countries are named as they were at the time: "West Germany" for the titles of 1954, 1974 and 1990 and for the 1974 host. Results up to and including the 2026 men's World Cup, won by Spain on 19 July 2026. Taken from Wikidata and checked against FIFA's own data and the RSSSF.

method: Research, drafting and cross-checking were done by AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks against live Wikidata and the app's SHACL/DCAT-AP validators; the deck is to be reviewed further by independent AI reviewers. The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert.

Finding the tournaments: the Wikidata items of the two competitions were found with the Wikidata search API (query 1): FIFA World Cup (Q19317) and FIFA Women's World Cup (Q19323). Query 2 selected every item whose P3450 (sports season of league or competition) is one of them, with start and end time (P580/P582), the truthy winner (P1346), country (P17) and the English and Swedish labels; the CSV was saved. Besides the tournaments it returned qualification groups, the unplayed 1942 and 1946 editions, future editions (2027 onward for women, 2030 onward for men) and the unofficial women's tournaments of 1970 and 1971.

Statements of all ranks: query 3 listed every P17, P276 and P1346 statement, with its rank, of the held editions 1930–2026. All are normal rank; every held edition has exactly one winner. Query 4 fetched the P17 and P1532 (country for sport) of the winning teams and of two locations, query 5 every English, Swedish and multilingual label and alias of the tournaments, teams and countries used, and query 6 the aliases of all the tournaments (the English "FIFA World Cup 1958" and Swedish "VM i fotboll 1958" forms on which the fronts are modelled).

The 2026 men's World Cup: the Wikidata item (Q5020214, fetched in full with query 7) gives the winner Spain (Q42267) without a reference, and its English description still read "being held". Because the tournament ended after the compiler's training data, the result was established from sources fetched on 2026-10-04: a web search for the final's result (news reports of Spain's 1–0 win over Argentina after extra time on 19 July 2026; discovery only, not cited; the exact search string of that first search was not recorded, and query 22 is the re-run made in QC round 3), then FIFA's own match data (query 8: the final of season 285023, Spain 1–0 Argentina, winner Spain), RSSSF's overview (query 10: "2026 Spain", "Spain 1-0 Argentina AET") and the Swedish Wikipedia introduction (query 12). Only the latter three are cited, as verification; the facts of the back note come from Wikidata's item of the final (Q55640701, query 17), which records the date, the teams, the 1–0 score, the winner and the goal in the second half of extra time.

Cross-check against FIFA: the script fifa_api.py (query 8, its source given in full) downloaded FIFA's public API list of seasons of competitions 17 (men) and 103 (women), each season's match list and the names of the host and winning teams, and printed each tournament's official name, host teams and final. For 1950, which had no final, the matches of the stage "Final Round" were listed (query 9). Every card was compared with this data: all 64 agree, under FIFA's own team names ("Germany FR", "Korea Republic", "USA", "China PR").

Cross-check against the RSSSF: the men's overview (query 10) gives the palmares, each final and the country of each final tournament; the women's overview and the RSSSF page of each Women's World Cup (query 11, rsssf_women.py, its source given in full; each page has its own author, credited in the source "rsssf-women-pages") give the palmares, the finals and in each page title the host. All 64 cards agree.

Team names as at the time: the cards name the winner and the host as the country the team or tournament represented at the time, the convention of FIFA's own records. For 1954, 1974 and 1990 the winner is West Germany (FIFA: "Germany FR", a team record of its own; RSSSF: "West Germany"), and the 1974 host is West Germany (FIFA's host team "Germany FR", although FIFA's tournament name is "1974 FIFA World Cup Germany"; RSSSF "[Final tournament in West Germany]"). Wikidata records these with the present-day items (the team Q43310, "Germany men's national association football team", and the country Germany, Q183); the West German names come from Wikidata's West Germany item (Q713750, en "West Germany", sv "Västtyskland") and the team's aliases "West Germany national football team" and "Västtysklands herrlandslag i fotboll". For 1966 the host is England, as FIFA ("1966 FIFA World Cup England™") and RSSSF name it; Wikidata's P17 is the United Kingdom (Q145), and the winner England comes from the team's P1532 (England, Q21). The West German name and dates of the notes come from Q713750 (its alias "Federal Republic of Germany (1949–1990)", P571, P576 and P1366); these checks confirm wording only. That the 1974 host was West Germany rests on FIFA's host team "Germany FR", RSSSF and the Swedish Wikipedia, not on a Wikidata statement. That West Germany won in 1954, 1974 and 1990 rests on the winner team of FIFA's final, "Germany FR", and on RSSSF ("West Germany"), not on a Wikidata statement (Wikidata has only the team's alias); the Swedish Wikipedia confirms the Swedish name (for 1974 its introduction gives the host only, and its infobox "Mästare" the winner).

English and Swedish text: the fronts are the compiler's own pattern "FIFA World Cup 1958: winner" / "VM i fotboll 1958: segrare" (host: "värdland"), and "FIFA Women's World Cup 2023: …" / "VM i fotboll för damer 2023: …", built from Wikidata's aliases of the tournaments (for those without such an alias the builder checks the label instead; see the checks). The backs are the English and Swedish Wikidata labels of the countries, except "China" (Wikidata's English label is "People's Republic of China"; the Swedish label is "Kina") and "West Germany" (see above). The United States is "USA" in Swedish (Wikidata's Swedish label). Several hosts are joined with "and"/"och" in FIFA's order (South Korea and Japan; Australia and New Zealand), the 2026 hosts in alphabetical order (Canada, Mexico and the United States / Kanada, Mexiko och USA, as on the Swedish Wikipedia).

Swedish check: the script svwiki.py (query 12, its source given in full) fetched, through the MediaWiki API, the introductions and current revision ids of the Swedish Wikipedia articles on the tournaments with a convention or a note; the quoted sentences, linked to their revisions, are in the cards' evidence ("Turneringen vanns av Västtyskland", "spelades i England", "arrangerades i Västtyskland", "spelades i Kina" …).

Notes: a back note in the compiler's own words was added only where it helps to answer or to avoid a wrong answer, and only with facts that Wikidata (the content source) gives, the verification sources confirming them: 1950 (no final; Uruguay won the four-team final round, Q989777, whose last match Uruguay v Brazil, Q754483, ended 2–1 on 16 July 1950; query 16), West Germany (1954, 1974 and 1990 winners, 1974 host: the Federal Republic of Germany of 1949–1990, Q713750), England as a country of the United Kingdom (1966, Q21 P31 Q3336843), the first World Cup with two hosts (2002) and the first with three hosts and 48 teams (2026), both from the count of P17 values and the P1132 of every edition (query 15), and the 2026 final (Q55640701). The first version also had notes with FIFA's names ("Germany FR", "1974 FIFA World Cup Germany", "2002 FIFA World Cup Korea/Japan") and the move of the 2003 Women's World Cup from China because of SARS; these rested on verification sources only and were removed in QC round 3. Each note's facts are in the evidence of its card.

Assembly: the throwaway helper script make_dossier.py (kept only in the compiler's scratch directory, not part of the record) built the cards from the saved responses, asserting for each card that the Wikidata winner and host, FIFA's final and host teams and RSSSF's palmares and host agree with the card, so a disagreement stops the build. The dossier's text (sources, method, selection, licensing) was written with a second throwaway helper, meta.py. Their Wikidata assertions are re-run by the builder's checks on every build; their FIFA and RSSSF comparisons are recorded card by card in the evidence and were repeated independently in QC rounds 1 and 3. Machine checks: for every card the builder checks against live Wikidata the English and Swedish front wording (an alias or the label of the tournament), the winner (P1346) or host (P17; for 2007 women the P276 location and its P17), the team's P1532 country for sport, and the English and Swedish labels of the country on the back. The deck was then validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (scripts/validate_sources.ts).

Review: three independent AI reviewers (Claude) checked the deck for factual accuracy, for language and language tags, and for licensing and documentation (QC rounds 1–3). The changes they led to (the title and description wording, the notes rebuilt on Wikidata facts, the RSSSF authors, the full FIFA terms, the scripts given in full, the shorter quotations) were made by the authoring agent and re-checked with the builder's Wikidata checks and the validators. No human subject expert has reviewed the cards.
selection: Every FIFA World Cup actually held from the first (Uruguay 1930) to the most recent (Canada, Mexico and the United States 2026), 23 tournaments, and every FIFA Women's World Cup from the first (China 1991) to the most recent (Australia and New Zealand 2023), 9 tournaments; two cards for each, the winner and the host country or countries: 64 cards. Left out: the World Cups of 1942 and 1946, which were not held; the unofficial women's tournaments of 1970 (Italy) and 1971 (Mexico), which were not organised by FIFA and are in Wikidata only as editions of Q19323 (RSSSF lists them among the unofficial tournaments before FIFA's first in 1991); the 2027 Women's World Cup (Brazil, June–July 2027) and all later tournaments, not yet played; qualification tournaments; runners-up, scores, venues and individual awards. The host card names countries, not cities or stadiums. Results are as of 2026-10-04.
licensing: The only content source is Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0: the selection of tournaments, the winner and host of each, the English and Swedish names of the tournaments and countries, and the facts in the back notes (the 1950 final round, the 2026 final, the number of hosts and teams, West Germany's dates, England in the United Kingdom) come from it, so the deck can be CC0 1.0 like the rest of the library. FIFA's data API and the RSSSF pages (all rights reserved; RSSSF's permission to copy with acknowledgement is not a recognised open licence and is not relied on) and the Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used for verification only: they confirmed facts the Wikidata data gave and the names used at the time; no wording, table, data set or selection was copied from them. FIFA's terms limit use of its content and API to private, non-commercial use on FIFA's platforms (§5.3) and forbid using FIFA content, names, logos or marks without written agreement (§6.2): the API was consulted privately, and the deck reproduces nothing of FIFA's: no FIFA data, text, logo or mark, and no official tournament name (the fronts use Wikidata's aliases, e.g. "FIFA World Cup 1958"; the competition's name appears only to identify it). The provenance report cites FIFA's responses (tournament names as FIFA gives them, team ids, dates and scores) as short factual references so the checks can be repeated. The selection is every held edition of two competitions, the complete set, not a choice taken from any list. Quotations in the provenance report's evidence are not part of the CC0 deck: they remain under their sources' licences (Wikipedia text CC BY-SA 4.0 by Wikipedia contributors, each linked to the quoted revision; FIFA's data all rights reserved; each RSSSF page © its named author and RSSSF, credited in the sources) and are short quotations of at most one sentence each, given only to make the verification checkable.

queries.query:
"""Fetch the FIFA World Cup and Women's World Cup seasons, their final matches and host teams from FIFA's public API.

Saves every raw response under ./fifa/ and prints a summary table.
"""
import json
import time
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
OUT = HERE / "fifa"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
API = "https://api.fifa.com/api/v3"


def get(url: str, name: str) -> dict:
    path = OUT / name
    if path.exists():
        return json.loads(path.read_text())
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r:
        data = r.read()
    path.write_bytes(data)
    time.sleep(0.3)
    return json.loads(data)


def name(x):
    return x[0]["Description"] if x else ""


team_names: dict[str, str] = {}


def team(tid: str) -> str:
    if tid not in team_names:
        t = get(f"{API}/teams/{tid}?language=en", f"team-{tid}.json")
        team_names[tid] = name(t.get("Name", []))
    return team_names[tid]


for comp in ("17", "103"):
    seasons = get(f"{API}/seasons?idCompetition={comp}&count=100&language=en", f"seasons-{comp}.json")["Results"]
    for s in sorted(seasons, key=lambda s: s["StartDate"]):
        sid = s["IdSeason"]
        hosts = [team(h["IdTeam"]) for h in s.get("HostTeams") or []]
        matches = get(f"{API}/calendar/matches?idCompetition={comp}&idSeason={sid}&count=500&language=en",
                      f"matches-{comp}-{sid}.json")["Results"]
        finals = [m for m in matches if name(m.get("StageName", [])).lower() == "final"]
        if finals:
            m = finals[-1]
            h, a = m["Home"], m["Away"]
            win = m.get("Winner")
            wname = team(win) if win else ""
            line = (f"{name(h.get('TeamName', []))} {m.get('HomeTeamScore')}-{m.get('AwayTeamScore')} "
                    f"{name(a.get('TeamName', []))} (pens {m.get('HomeTeamPenaltyScore')}-{m.get('AwayTeamPenaltyScore')}) "
                    f"{m.get('Date')} winner={wname} stadium={name((m.get('Stadium') or {}).get('Name', []))}")
        else:
            stages = sorted({name(m.get("StageName", [])) for m in matches})
            line = f"NO FINAL; stages {stages}; {len(matches)} matches"
        print(comp, sid, name(s["Name"]), "| hosts:", hosts, "|", line)

"""Download RSSSF's page for each FIFA Women's World Cup 1991-2023 and print its title and first heading lines."""
import html
import re
import time
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
for f in ["wwc91f", "wwc95f", "wwc99f", "wwc03f", "wwc07f", "wwc2011f", "wwc2015f", "wwc2019f", "wwc2023f"]:
    url = f"https://www.rsssf.org/tablesw/{f}.html"
    path = HERE / f"rsssf-{f}.html"
    if not path.exists():
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as r:
            path.write_bytes(r.read())
        time.sleep(1)
    t = path.read_text(encoding="latin-1")
    title = re.search(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", t, re.I | re.S)
    body = html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", "", t))
    lines = [l.strip() for l in body.splitlines() if l.strip()][:4]
    print(url, "|", title.group(1).strip() if title else "", "|", " / ".join(lines))
